flagship.headline: The Who begin recording Tommy at IBC Studios
flagship.summary_line_1: The Who arrived at IBC Studios in London on September 19, 1968, to begin the sessions that would become Tommy, Pete Townshend's ambitious rock opera about a deaf, dumb, and blind pinball-playing boy.
flagship.summary_line_2: The album took six months to finish and turned the band from singles act into stadium headliners, with Pinball Wizard becoming one of the record's signature tracks.

events.headline: Creedence Clearwater Revival score their only UK number one
events.summary_line_1: Bad Moon Rising by Creedence Clearwater Revival topped the UK Singles Chart on September 19, 1969, and held the spot for three weeks.
events.summary_line_2: It remains the only UK number one of the band's career, a stark warning-siren single John Fogerty wrote after watching the 1941 film The Devil and Daniel Webster.

events.headline: Fleetwood Mac release Then Play On
events.summary_line_1: Fleetwood Mac released their third studio album, Then Play On, in the UK on September 19, 1969, the last studio record to feature founding guitarist Peter Green.
events.summary_line_2: The album fused heavy blues with folk and progressive instrumentals, including Green's own Oh Well, and pointed toward the band's later sound even as Green left the group the following year.

events.headline: The Who begin recording Tommy at IBC Studios
events.summary_line_1: The Who arrived at IBC Studios in London on September 19, 1968, to begin the sessions that would become Tommy, Pete Townshend's ambitious rock opera about a deaf, dumb, and blind pinball-playing boy.
events.summary_line_2: The album took six months to finish and turned the band from singles act into stadium headliners, with Pinball Wizard becoming one of the record's signature tracks.

events.headline: Red Foley dies in Fort Wayne at 58
events.summary_line_1: Country and gospel star Red Foley suffered respiratory failure and died in his sleep in Fort Wayne, Indiana, hours after playing two shows there on September 19, 1968.
events.summary_line_2: Foley had already shaped country music for two decades, discovering Brenda Lee and hosting the pioneering television show Ozark Jubilee before his death at 58.

events.headline: Bee Gees release Massachusetts in the UK
events.summary_line_1: Polydor released the Bee Gees' Massachusetts in the United Kingdom on September 19, 1967, a lush ballad the Gibb brothers wrote in New York and originally intended for the Seekers.
events.summary_line_2: The song became the group's first UK number one and went on to top the charts in a dozen other countries, part of the same British pop wave as the British Invasion bands a few years earlier.

events.headline: Dino, Desi & Billy perform I'm a Fool on Ed Sullivan
events.summary_line_1: Teenage pop trio Dino, Desi & Billy, the sons of Dean Martin and Desi Arnaz plus their friend Billy Hinsche, performed their hit I'm a Fool live on The Ed Sullivan Show on September 19, 1965.
events.summary_line_2: The clean-cut, organ-driven single fit neatly into the era's pop and Brill Building sound and gave the young band its widest television audience yet.

events.headline: Future country star Trisha Yearwood is born in Monticello, Georgia
events.summary_line_1: Patricia Lynn Yearwood was born in Monticello, Georgia, on September 19, 1964, the daughter of a schoolteacher and a small-town banker.
events.summary_line_2: She would not release her breakthrough single until 1991, but Yearwood went on to become one of country music's defining vocalists, decades after the genre's 1960s foundations were laid.

events.headline: Beatles celebrate Brian Epstein's 30th birthday over Missouri
events.summary_line_1: Flying from their Dallas concert to a rest day at Reed Pigman's ranch in Alton, Missouri, the Beatles sang Happy Birthday to manager Brian Epstein just after midnight on September 19, 1964, and gave him an antique telephone.
events.summary_line_2: The celebration continued at the ranch, where their host had baked a cake with thirty candles, a rare quiet moment near the end of the Beatles' grueling first North American tour.

image.alt: Brian Epstein photographed in the Netherlands, 1965

events.headline: Future Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker is born in Sheffield
events.summary_line_1: Jarvis Cocker was born in Sheffield, England, on September 19, 1963, decades before he would front the Britpop band Pulp.
events.summary_line_2: Cocker grew up on the British Invasion sound coming out of Liverpool and London, and he later credited that 1960s songwriting craft as a direct influence on his own sharp, observational lyrics.

events.headline: Ann-Margret voices Ann-Margrock on The Flintstones
events.summary_line_1: Ann-Margret guest-starred as the singing sensation Ann-Margrock in the Flintstones episode Ann-Margrock Presents, which aired on ABC on September 19, 1963.
events.summary_line_2: She performed two songs in the episode, including I Ain't Gonna Be Your Fool No More, bringing a real pop star's voice into Saturday morning's biggest cartoon.

events.headline: Sherry holds number one as Surfin' Safari climbs the WMCA survey
events.summary_line_1: New York's WMCA Good Guys Survey dated September 19, 1962 had the Four Seasons' Sherry sitting at number one while the Beach Boys' Surfin' Safari climbed to number two.
events.summary_line_2: The pairing captured a hinge moment in early 1960s pop, polished East Coast vocal harmony sharing the airwaves with the raw new California surf sound.

events.headline: Yevtushenko publishes Babi Yar, later inspiring Shostakovich's 13th Symphony
events.summary_line_1: Soviet poet Yevgeny Yevtushenko published Babi Yar in the newspaper Literaturnaya Gazeta on September 19, 1961, confronting Soviet silence around the Nazi massacre of Kiev's Jewish population and lingering antisemitism at home.
events.summary_line_2: Composer Dmitri Shostakovich later set the poem as the opening movement of his Symphony No. 13, a piece so politically charged that Soviet authorities pressured performers to avoid it.

events.headline: Chubby Checker's The Twist hits number one
events.summary_line_1: Chubby Checker's cover of The Twist reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100 on September 19, 1960, a song originally written and recorded by Hank Ballard and the Midnighters two years earlier.
events.summary_line_2: The Twist returned to number one again in January 1962, the only song in Hot 100 history to top the chart in two separate, non-consecutive runs.

events.headline: Hank Ballard and the Midnighters land three songs on the Hot 100 at once
events.summary_line_1: The same week Chubby Checker's cover hit number one, Hank Ballard and the Midnighters became the first group in Billboard history to place three singles on the Hot 100 at once, Finger Poppin' Time, Let's Go, Let's Go, Let's Go, and their own original version of The Twist.
events.summary_line_2: Ballard had refused to perform The Twist on national television, which is why Dick Clark turned to Chubby Checker for the cover that made the dance a craze.
